Title: The Goose Programming Language · Goose
Thank you, but I prefer it my way
Description: The LLMs have changed how software gets made, and will keep changing it - for code, for design, for any digital product. Buried under all the productivity talk there is one thing they enable which does not get discussed much: never having to collaborate with another human being, ever again. The library whose maintainer won’t answer, the framework whose author finds your use case silly, the colleague who wants it done just so - you can now route around all of them. You can rewrite the thing in an afternoon, and nobody gets to tell you “no”. We may soon come to regret this new freedom. Not because the rewrites are bad (they are often fine), but because the thing that forced us to work together is gone - and both sides of the open source bargain have spent years making sure we wouldn’t miss it.

Title: Indian government sites are serving revoked eMudhra certificates
Description: On 17th October, eight eMudhra intermediate CAs chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 were found to have trivially recoverable private keys. They were revoked the next day, and Mozilla and Chrome are now distrusting the G3 root. Separately, on 19th October eMudhra revoked 9,356 certificates on its unaffected RSA hierarchy (emSign Root CA - G1) with the reason “Superseded”. That batch matches every unexpired certificate missing a certificate-type policy OID required by emSign’s own CP/CPS (Bug 2082782).

Title: The glorious @xkcdRandom Zig builtin
Description: One of my favorite xkcd comics of all time is Random Number. The image depicts a C function that supposedly returns a random integer, but in reality always returns 4. I was reminded of this wonderful comic a few days ago, due to a security incident where people accidentally used the number 4 (among others) instead of a properly generated sequence of random bytes. Satire has a tendency to become reality, I guess.
